 ATP Finals Alexander Zverev v Ben Shelton: ATP Finals tennis group stage – live
 🎾 ATP Finals updates, with play from 7.30pm GMT
 🎾 Sign up for the Recap newsletter | Email Daniel 
 LIVE  Updated  3m ago Daniel Harris Tue 17 Nov 2026 15.23 EST First published on Tue 17 Nov 2026 13.30 EST Share Key events 2h ago Preamble 
 Alexander Zverev fires off a forehand to Ben Shelton. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters View image in fullscreen Alexander Zverev fires off a forehand to Ben Shelton. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Daniel Harris Tue 17 Nov 2026 15.23 EST First published on Tue 17 Nov 2026 13.30 EST Share Key events 2h ago Preamble 
 2m ago 15.23 EST *Zverev 6-2 Shelton Ace down the middle, 15-0; big serve out wide, return doesn’t reach the net, 30-0; my screen jumps, 40-0; then a decent forehand from Shelton, on to Zverev’s tootsies gives him a light sniff. Oh, and Shelton then draws him to net, his volleys, though improved, still a weakness … and clumsy backhand effort wafts long; 40-30. This is better from Shelton, decent return then helping him to deuce and three sett points saved … but that big ace down the T raises another … then yet another secures a dominant first set for Zverev. Shelton has a lot of thinking to do and not long in which to do it.
 Share 9m ago 15.16 EST Zverev 5-2 Shelton* Serving to stay in the first set, Shelton opens with a service winner, then pays a decent point from the back, perhaps his best of the match so far, for 30-0. A backhand return hooked wide means 40-0, then a slam-dunk overhead followed by another forces Zverev to serve out the set.
 Share 12m ago 15.13 EST *Zverev 5-1 Shelton Shane Warne once said that Brian Lara was the third-best batter in the world, behind Sachin Tendulkar and daylight, and similar is so of men’s tennis, I think. Daylight is third, behind Alcaraz and Sinner, but also fifth, between Zverev and the rest. Over the next few years, I’m excited to see if Jodar and Joao Fonseca make thigs more interesting, Mensik and Lehecka too, but back with our match, Zverev misses with a hopeful forehand down the line to give 30-all. We know what’s coming next, though, a service winner dematerialised out wide, then one down the T sets up a rally that’s quickly finished.
 View image in fullscreen Alexander Zverev smashes a serve to Ben Shelton. Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/Reuters Share Updated at  15.16 EST 18m ago 15.08 EST Zverev 4-1 Shelton* The problem for Shelton – I think – is that he’s got to keep holding. The way the rallies are going, I fear for his ability to do that and, as I type, a double donates 0-30; big trouble. Gosh, and when he runs to net to put away a volley, he overhits and, at 0-40, having spurned two break points he now faces three. The first is saved with a big first serve then he gets away with a second that sits up, Zverev failing to middle his return then framing the second ball. But Shelton then nets a buggy-whip forehand, and I’m afraid this set is racing away from him.
 Share 21m ago 15.04 EST *Zverev 3-1 Shelton Before Zverev serves, Shelton’s old fella tells him to move forward at the first opportunity … easier said than done, given the quality of the first serves. But that’s exactly what he does, a forehand down the line opening the court for the winner … then a huge serve is punished back via forehand for 0-30! This is much better from the American and, though Zverev wins the next point, Shelton stays in the one after long enough to benefit from the error, and inside-out backhand flying wide for 15-40. This is a chance, all the more so when Zverev misses his first first serve of the match … but the return hits the tape, Shelton attacking it as he needed to only to miss the target. Next up, an ace, and from there, the hold is swiftly secured. Still, this is more of a contest now.
 Share 28m ago 14.58 EST Zverev 2-1 Shelton* Shelton comes in … and is caught by a backhand pass, but a decent inside-out forehand to the corner makes 15-all. An ace on to the outermost fibre of the T … is followed by another down the middle, 140mph, and this is more like it, but does he have anything besides the serve? Zverev immediately assumes control of the next rally and even when he plays to the wrong side, Shelton can’t steer his riposte into court, and another decent return takes us to deuce. Whereupon Zverev lands a deep return then slashes a backhand cross for advantage; Shelton responds with a third ace of the game, 144mph. But he just can’t stick in the rallies, his balls too short and sitting up to be assaulted; again, he goes down advantage, but again he finds an ace when he needs one … then another. That’s five in the game now, except he still can’t finish the game off, a second serve handed the treatment and deuce restored. This time, though, Shelton sees it out, and he’s on the board – but the way the rallies are going, you fear for him if he doesn’t improve.
 View image in fullscreen Ben Shelton bashes a backhand to Alexander Zverev. Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP Share Updated at  15.17 EST 36m ago 14.50 EST *Zverev 2-0 Shelton Already, Shelton must break to avoid losing the first set – Rafael Jodar couldn’t in the first round of matches – and two colossal serves quickly raise 30-0. An even bigger ace down the T follows, then Shelton goes long on the backhand, and that’s the consolidation in double-quick time.
 Share 38m ago 14.48 EST Zverev 1-0 Shelton* (*denotes server) Zverev guides an inside-out forehand into the corner, but is then cramped by a body-serve – one way to take away the long-arm advantage he talked about after the US Open final. And he then makes 15-30, only for a return into the net to restore parity. Shelton, though, swats a backhand fractionally long, Zverev having targeted it with shape, raising break point … and a leaping forehand into the net converts it. Every rally that got going, the world No 1 won.
 Share 41m ago 14.44 EST Ready … play. 
 Share 43m ago 14.43 EST Shelton’s backhand was pretty nifty against Arthur Fils in his first match. If it’s on tonight, he’s got a much better chance of winning – and it’s something Juan Carlos Ferrero must sort with him if he’s to improve on his current standing in the game.
 Share Updated at  14.44 EST 46m ago 14.40 EST Zverev elects to receive. Neither play will want to lose, obviously, but neither player will especially want to lose in tow as, that could be a tiebreaker in the event of a tie at the top. Because three players have now won a match, there are too many permutations to go into at this point and neither of these two are out with a defeat; we’ll investigate how things stand at the end.
 Share Updated at  14.44 EST 51m ago 14.35 EST Here come our players… 
 View image in fullscreen Alexander Zverev waves as he enters the arena … Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP View image in fullscreen Whilst Ben Shelton sports a steely stare. Photograph: Luca Bruno/AP Share Updated at  15.06 EST 52m ago 14.33 EST Despite the below, I’m excited to see how Shelton goes about this. If he can find whip on his forehand cross, perhaps he can force Zverev far enough out of court to take away his backhand while opening up the court for winners.
 Share 1h ago 14.29 EST I’ve had to concede defeat; I can’t find Henry’s excellent speech about the future of doubles anywhere, but the gist is that it’s a form of the game widely played and loved. If given support, it will thrive, and it brings people in as it; just look at how busy Wimbledon is in week two.
 Share 1h ago 14.15 EST Regular readers will know Calv coaches Henry Patten, with his partner Harri Heloivaara, men’s doubles winner at Wimbledon this year – for the second time. Regular readers may also know that the ATP are currently seeking to take careers and money away from doubles players to give to already exceedingly well remunerated singles players, a move against which Henry is leading the righteous fight.
 Yesterday, when the pair were honoured for finishing the year at world No 1s, Henry pointed out that the ATP’s CEO and chair were conspicuous by their absences. So the ATP then edited that bit out before posting it on their own socials, and endeavoured to have it taken down under copyright infringement where others had.

 Allow and continue Share 1h ago 14.09 EST Oh and Coach Calv gets in touch to point out that, in his opinion and contradicting my earlier thoughts, Shelton’s two strengths, his serve and forehand cross, play into Zverev’s, retuern and backhand.
 Share 1h ago 14.07 EST Er, I spent some time this afternoon researching my earlier optimism we’d see a contest, and this is what I found: 
 I didn’t see Zverev’s opening match as I was on the football, but he got 85% his first serves in. If he does that again, at the pace he sends them down, there’s not much Shelton can do.
 Shelton is considered to have a big forehand, but the metrics say otherwise. At 78mph, he’s level with the tour average on speed and his average spin is just 43rpm above tour average.
 On return, he was, just after the US Open, 85th on return metrics taken from the top 100 in the world.
 Which, given his well documented issues on the backhand – he gets it in but can’t do much with it – doesn’t leave much beyond his serve. Talking of which, if his serve +1 is a forehand, he has an 80% better chance of winning the point than if it’s a backhand so, even with a decent serve, if he’s then made to his a backhand, he tends to lose the rally.
 Share Updated at  14.13 EST 2h ago 13.30 EST Preamble
 “Achieving the world No 1 status is something every player dreams of, but I feel like I’m the only world No 1 in tennis history that has to explain why it’s OK for me to be world No 1. Which I find quite difficult, because I think I deserve to be where I am”.
 So said Alexander Zverev after becoming the first world No 1 to lose in straight sets immediately after establishing that status. He does, though, know why it’s like this. First of all, not everyone agrees with his assertion that “the accusations” against him of domestic violence “have been proven false”, so not everyone is happy with his new status. But there are sporting reasons too: the man unable to win majors when Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz are healthy has pirated two in their absence, beating no one ranked higher than 14 to take the first and no one ranked higher than nine to take the second. A such, he sits inside a tautological paradox: a win is a win, yet also, there are wins and there are wins.
 Zverev has, though, collected this trophy twice – hard court, best of three sets, is probably his sweet spot – and will expect to beat Ben Shelton tonight, his serve and backhand, two of the best shots in the game, likely to be definitive. Shelton, though, is growing, his win over Alcaraz in New York the biggest of his career, and though he was easily despatched in the final by Zverev, who leads their head-to-head 6-0, there’s a sense a move is being made. He’s taken a new coach in Juan Carlos Ferrero and with it a new confidence that the right things are being done, improvement imminent.
 Whether he’s changed quickly enough is uncertain. But his lefty angle, correctly deployed, might hamper Zverev’s backhand, just as the flat forehand down the line might test his weaker flank – and, if he’s to rise beyond his current station, at 24 these are the matches he needs to start winning, and soon.
 Play: 8.30pm local, 7.30pm GMT
